segments.text: Have you ever looked at an  Excel spreadsheet and wondered,
"Where do I even start?" The numbers blur into  a maze of confusion, and the data seems like
an unsolvable riddle. All while the clock is  ticking on your deadline, the good news is,
as a data analyst, you don't necessarily  need to use complex programming languages
like Python or R. In this video, I'm going  to show you a real-world example of how
we can use Excel to automate gathering and  cleaning data, analyzing and exploring data,
and then visualizing your findings in a dashboard.  The link to the file download is in the video
description so you can follow along. But before  we get started, I've got a quick question for you:
What is the one Excel feature or function that you  wish you understood better? Share your thoughts in
the comments. I love hearing from you, and  your answers might inspire our next video.
You've been given 11 months' worth of  sales data, and your boss has asked
you to summarize and analyze it because she  doesn't think gross profit is as high as it
should be given the sales volume. The  sales data is categorized by segment,
country, product, discount band, and  manager. To add to the challenge,
the data is spread across 11 separate Excel files  encompassing January to November, and you need to
be prepared to include December's data when it  becomes available in a couple of weeks' time.
I'm going to use Power Query to get these files  from the folder and consolidate them into one
table. So, on the Data tab of the ribbon,  go to Get Data > From File > From Folder,
and then browse to the folder containing  your files and click Open. Here,
you get a preview of the files  in the folder. Click on Combine,
and then Combine and Transform Data because  I still have some more data cleaning to do.
Here it's showing me the first file and then  the sheets in that file. I only have one sheet,
and it gives me a preview on the right.  I'll click OK, and this opens the Power
Query Editor window. On the left, I  have the queries Power Query created
to combine the files and then the final  query that contains the combined data,
which is currently selected. I'm going to collapse  the pane as I don't need to do anything with it.
Here, I have a preview of the data, and the first  column contains the file name. I need to extract
the date from the file name because my data  tables don't have a separate date column. So,
on the Transform tab, I'm going to Replace  Values. Here, I want to find ".xlsx" and
replace it with nothing. Click OK. Then  I'll change the data type from text to date,
and now each file's data is tagged  with the first date of the month it
relates to. I'll double-click to rename  the column, and we'll call it "date."
Next, I'm going to replace "The United States of  America" with "USA" because this is going to take
up less space in my reports. So, we'll Replace  Values. Now, Power Query is case-sensitive,
so be sure to enter this exactly as  it appears in the data set. Click OK.
All right, next, I've got some fractions in  my "Unit Sold" column that can't be right. So,
let's fix that on the Transform tab,  rounding, and I'm going to round up.
Now, I need to investigate profitability,  so let's add a column to calculate the gross
profit percent. I'm going to select  "Profit" (holding down Control),
select "Sales," and then we're going to add a  column. Under standard, we want to divide. Now,
I can rename this column by double-clicking here,  or I can simply rename it in the formula bar. So,
this is going to be "GP %," and I'll  change the data type to percentage.
All right, next, I'll add a column  to calculate the discount. So,
I want to select the "Discount %"  column and then "Gross Sales," standard,
and divide. Let's rename this one "Discount %,"  and we'll change the data type to percentage.
Okay, our data is ready, and  notice in the "Applied Steps" pane,
Power Query has recorded each step, so when  I add December's data, I can include it with
the click of a single button. I'll rename  the query "Data," and on the Home tab,
we're going to "Close and Load To," and  I want a table on a new sheet. Click OK.
Notice the formatting for the percentage  columns didn't come through, and that's
because the data type setting,  which we applied in Power Query,
isn't the same as a cell format.  So, let's apply some formatting.
As you can see, Power Query is super efficient  at gathering and cleaning data. If you want to
use Power Query in other areas of your work  to improve productivity by automating boring
and laborious tasks like these, check out my  course linked to in the video description.
Now that we've gathered and cleaned  the data, let's get an overview of
what we're working with. We can use the Data  Analysis tool on the Data tab of the ribbon,
over on the far right, to automatically create  some key statistics. If you don't have it,
go to the File tab and then at the very bottom,  Options, and then Add-ins, and then click Go,
and select "Analysis ToolPak," and click OK.  It should now be available on the Data tab.
There are a lot of statistical tools available  in the Data Analysis ToolPak. The one I want
is "Descriptive Statistics," so click OK.  I'm going to start by looking at the gross
profit column. So, my input range is  "Gross Profit," and it's in a column,
and it has the label in the first row. I'm  going to put it on my "Summary Statistics"
page in this cell here, and then I want summary  statistics. I'll click OK, and now I have a
table that summarizes the characteristics of  the data set, including the mean or average,
the median, mode, minimum, maximum,  and count of records in the data set,
plus some more advanced statistical measures that  describe the dispersion and shape of the data.
Let's get the statistics for the discount percent.  The Data Analysis Descriptive Statistics here,
I want the "Discount" column, and I'm going to put  it here and click OK. Now, if it's easier to read,
I can apply a percentage format and then  copy that format across to the table.
We can also use the Analysis ToolPak  to generate a histogram that shows the
number of discounts in bands. But one of the  problems with this tool is it doesn't retain
a connection to the source data. So when  I update the file with December's data,
I have to run through these steps again.  A better way is with a pivot table.
On the Data sheet, I'm going to insert a  pivot table, and I'm going to put it on
the "Summary Statistics" sheet. We'll just pop  it here, and here, I want to see my discount
percent in the values and in the rows, and I'm  going to group the discounts into bands of 2%,
and I want to see them summarized by  count. Let's go and insert a column
chart. I'll just bring it up here, and I'll select  the columns, Ctrl+1, to edit, and we're going to
change the Gap width to zero, and now we have  a histogram. I'll quickly remove the legend and
add data labels and remove the vertical axis;  we don't need that now, and the grid lines.
I'll give the chart a title, "Count  of Discounts by Band." We can see
from this chart that discounts at the  higher end are still quite frequent,
and these will be having a  significant effect on gross profit.
Like I mentioned earlier, the descriptive  statistics tables don't retain a connection to
the data. So when we add data for December, you'll  have to run through these steps again. However,
there are some other options for generating  summary statistics that can be updated,
and I cover them in this more comprehensive  video. So bookmark that for later.
Now that we have a feel for  the data we're working with,
it's time to dig deeper to get to the bottom  of the areas gross profit is underperforming.
A fast way for Microsoft 365 users to get  insights into their data is with the built-in
AI tool. You'll find it on the Home tab of  the ribbon, and it's called "Analyze Data."
Analyze Data scans your data for trends, patterns,  and outliers, and it can be helpful to not only
get a feel for the errors that account  for the majority of your sales or profit,
but it's also great at identifying insights  not immediately obvious when working with large
amounts of data. For example, here it's found  that the segment "Enterprise" has noticeably
lower gross profit. So let's insert that, and  then I'll click here to show all 35 results.
It's also found that gross profit is relatively  even across managers, so there's no one manager
causing the problem here. It's found that sales  and gross profit appear to cluster into two groups
with four outliers, which might be something  to dig deeper into. So let's insert that,
and I'm just going to Ctrl+X and cut it  out and put it on my "Insights" page.
Let's see what else it's found. Here,  it's found gross profit is relatively
even across countries, so there's  no one country causing the problem.
Now, we can also ask it to focus on a specific  area of our data. For example, let's say I want
insights for discount by segment, and it's found  that government and small business have noticeably
higher discounts. So let's insert that. Let's  move the charts, I'll cut them out and paste
them onto this sheet here. And this one. And let's just roughly resize them.
If you don't have Analyze Data, you can analyze  your data with formulas or pivot tables,
which I prefer because they're super fast to  build. If you're not confident with pivot tables,
you can go to your data sheet,  and then on the "Insert" tab,
we have recommended pivot tables. They open in  a task pane on the right, and you can click the
insert buttons to place them on a new sheet or  an existing sheet. Then, you can work with them
like a pivot table you built from scratch,  changing colors, making modifications, etc.
Or if you have Analyze Data, you can also ask  it to build you a pivot table. For example,
show me the average gross profit by  country and product in a pivot table,
and just like that, it's done. Let's insert it,
and I'm just going to Ctrl X to cut it out,  and we'll put it on the "Insights" tab.
Now I'm going to switch country and product  around, and I'm going to sort it smallest
to largest, and let's quickly change the  style. We'll just make it this light color,
and we'll apply some formatting. So on the  Home tab, conditional formatting, color scales,
and I want green through red, and then let's  apply it to all cells showing the average of
gross profit percent values for country and  product, and now we can easily see areas
with lower gross profit margins. If I want to  see the transactions that make up the value,
I can double click on the cell, and it takes me  to a data sheet that has all the transactions.
Let's look at the data another way. I'll copy  this pivot table, and we'll paste underneath,
and instead of country, let's look at it  by segment, and again, we're going to sort
smallest to largest. Let's add some conditional  formatting, and bingo! We can now see that
the problem areas are Enterprise and small  business, and channel partners are more than
double mid-market and government, so we might want  to investigate how they achieve those results.
I'm going to copy this pivot table, and we'll  paste it here. Move that across, and instead
of gross profit, I want discount percent,  and I want to see it summarized by average,
and let's apply some number formatting. We want  a percentage with one decimal place. All right,
let's sort this one, this time largest to  smallest, and we'll apply some conditional
formatting, and this time I want red through  green. Okay, we can see a few areas to look
at. Let's copy that, and this time, instead of  country, let's look at it by segment, and let's
make sure the sorting is correct, smallest  to largest, and we'll apply the conditional
formatting red through green. Interestingly,  the discount percentage by product and segment
doesn't follow the same pattern as gross profit  percent, so we have some more digging to do,
but this will do for now. As you can see,  pivot tables make light work of data analysis.
Okay, let's see how we handle adding December's  data to this report. I'll add December's file
to the folder. We'll go back to Excel, and  on the data tab, I'm going to click "Refresh
All," and just like that, all our visuals on this  insights page update. The only things that don't
update are the descriptive statistics we created  using the data analysis tool. As a data analyst,
the next tool you should explore is Power Pivot.  Now a lot of people get confused about the
difference between Power Query and Power Pivot and  when to use them, so check out this video next.
